title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a clinicoradiographic neurovascular disorder characterized by acute or subacute onset of seizures, encephalopathy, headache, and visual disturbances, often occurring in the setting of uncontrolled or rapidly rising blood pressure. Although classically associated with posterior cerebral white matter edema on imaging, PRES can involve multiple brain regions and is not always reversible. Prompt recognition is essential, as delayed diagnosis and treatment may result in permanent neurologic deficits, epilepsy, or life-threatening complications. Risk factors include hypertension, renal disease, autoimmune disorders, preeclampsia, sepsis, and exposure to cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapies.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course reviews the clinical features, diagnostic studies, and management of PRES across diverse clinical settings. Participants will also gain an understanding of key clinical predictors, the interpretation of neuroimaging findings, the distinction between PRES and stroke and other mimics, and the implementation of safe blood pressure and seizure management strategies. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying PRES early in its clinical course, etiologic assessment, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition to reduce morbidity and improve neurologic outcomes.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the clinical features of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome that should facilitate prompt evaluation. Evaluate underlying etiologies of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome to guide targeted treatment and prevent recurrence. Collaborate management strategies with interprofessional team members to improve care coordination and improve outcomes for patients with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a clinicoradiographically diagnosed neurovascular disorder, also known as reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy syndrome (RPLS) and hyperperfusion encephalopathy. Individuals with PRES can present with altered mentation or stupor, drowsiness, visual disturbances, eg, visual hallucinations, cortical blindness, hemianopia, quadrantanopia, and diplopia, seizures that may be focal or generalized tonic-clonic, and headaches. [1] PRES can develop acutely or subacutely, with symptoms emerging within hours to days. Presentations often occur in the setting of acute uncontrolled hypertension, with systolic blood pressures of 160 mm Hg and above, commonly ranging from 160 to 190 mm Hg. [2]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Introduction
content: The designation of PRES reflects both its clinical and radiographic features. Radiographically, MRI commonly reveals white matter edema, appearing as hyperintense T2 signals or hypointense T1 signals, most frequently in the posterior cerebrum symmetrically, though asymmetric patterns can occur. The term PRES also emphasizes the potential reversibility of symptoms when recognition and prompt treatment occur. However, the syndrome’s name can be misleading, as edema does not always localize to the posterior cerebral white matter. Edema can extend beyond the parietal-occipital regions into watershed zones, involve the thalamus, and occasionally affect the anterior circulation. [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] PRES does not always resolve, and some patients may experience life-threatening complications, eg, transforaminal cerebellar herniation or focal neurologic deficits, particularly if treatment is delayed. [3] [7]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Individuals at risk for developing PRES often have 1 or more contributing factors, triggers, or underlying etiologies. Common risk factors include hypertension, rapid rises in blood pressure, preeclampsia, kidney disease such as nephrotic syndrome—which can cause hypovolemia and secondary hypertension through activation of the renin-angiotensin system—renal failure, and liver disease. Exposure to certain chemotherapy agents, including platinum-containing medications, gemcitabine, and CHOP/R-CHOP regimens (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin [doxorubicin], oncovin [vincristine], and prednisone), as well as cytotoxic medications or immunosuppressants, eg, tacrolimus, sirolimus, interferon therapies, and various immunotherapies or monoclonal antibodies, eg, bevacizumab, pazopanib, sorafenib, and sunitinib, also increases risk. [3] [8] [9] [10] [11]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Autoimmune disorders, including hemolytic uremic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus, as well as sepsis or allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, further contribute to PRES susceptibility. [2] [12] [13] [14] [15] Among these triggers and etiologies, uncontrolled hypertension occurs most frequently; however, acute hypertension alone does not predict PRES development, and identifying which hypertensive individuals will progress to PRES remains challenging. [2] [16]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: PRES is a historically underdiagnosed syndrome, perhaps due to limited awareness; however, with the increasing availability of imaging and improvements in its quality, awareness of PRES has increased, and an understanding of its epidemiology has emerged. Based on several reports and studies, PRES affects people of all ages but is more common in middle-aged women. [1] [6] [17]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: In a retrospective study involving the review of demographics, risk factors, and clinical presentation of 113 people with PRES, Fugate and colleagues found that 51 individuals (45%) had an autoimmune disease with most of the individuals presenting with seizures (74%), followed by encephalopathy (28%), headache (26%), and visual disturbance (20%). [4] Having an epileptic seizure at presentation was found to be the best predictor for PRES, and encephalopathy was the second-best predictor. The same study found that having a recent exposure to chemotherapy and those with underlying renal failure were also crucial predictors of PRES. [18]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathophysiology of PRES remains incompletely understood, but dysregulation of cerebral autoregulation has been proposed as a central mechanism. [2] Cerebral autoregulation maintains constant cerebral blood flow across a range of blood pressures by adjusting vascular resistance. When blood pressure rises, typically above a systolic pressure of 160 mm Hg in most individuals, maximal vasoconstriction occurs, and cerebral blood flow begins to increase with further pressure elevation. Elevated hydrostatic pressure can disrupt the blood-brain barrier, allowing intravascular fluid to leak into brain tissue and produce vasogenic edema. The posterior circulation appears particularly susceptible, likely due to fewer adaptive mechanisms that regulate fluid extravasation and barrier integrity under high blood pressure compared with the anterior circulation. [19] Findings from a formaldehyde histofluorescence study by Edvinsson and colleagues demonstrated a greater density of adrenergic perivascular fibers in the anterior circulation, suggesting that enhanced sympathetic innervation supports more robust autoregulation. [19] [20]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Critiques of the hypertensive-hyperperfusion hypothesis note that some individuals with PRES present with blood pressures below the brain's autoregulatory threshold. [1] [21] Not all cases involve hypertension. Case reports document PRES in normotensive patients receiving cytotoxic therapies, eg, tacrolimus after liver transplantation, supporting the role of endothelial dysfunction in disease development. [1] [3] [22] Tacrolimus, cyclosporine, cisplatin, and other immunosuppressants can directly damage the endothelium, compromising the blood-brain barrier. [19] [3]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Endothelial compromise also arises from neuroinflammation, as seen in sepsis, metabolic disorders, eg, uremia and hypomagnesemia, and autoimmune diseases. Astrogliosis, microgliosis, and endothelial activation in sepsis, along with endothelial injury in ANCA-associated vasculitides, increase blood-brain barrier permeability, promoting extravasation of intravascular fluid and facilitating PRES. [15] [23] [24] [25]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Ischemia has also been proposed as a contributing mechanism. Dysregulated autoregulation could lead to vasoconstriction and cytotoxic edema, with some radionuclide studies showing vasoconstriction in affected patients. [26] [27] [28] [29] However, these findings reflect a minority of cases, and subsequent pathology studies have largely failed to demonstrate ischemia or infarction. [30]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: PRES requires a clinical and radiographic diagnosis, making a thorough history and physical examination essential. Clinical presentations vary in both severity and acuity, with the most common symptoms including seizures in 80% of patients, headache in 50%, visual disturbances in 39%—eg, binocular diplopia, vision loss, no light perception, hemianopia, or quadrantanopia—encephalopathy in 28%, and focal neurological deficits in 10% to 15%. [31] Patients may present with altered mental status, limiting the reliability of their history, which makes obtaining collateral information from relatives, friends, or caregivers especially valuable.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Most patients present with moderately to severely elevated blood pressure, with up to 75% affected, although a small subset may remain normotensive. [21] Clinicians should pay particular attention to individuals experiencing rapid increases in blood pressure, as this can trigger PRES. [11] Physical examination should include assessment for hemianopia, quadrantanopia, visual neglect, cortical blindness, horizontal gaze palsy with intact vestibulo-ocular reflex, papilledema, oral trauma (eg, tongue biting during seizures), brisk reflexes, active convulsions, and urinary or fecal incontinence. [32] [33]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Imaging remains essential and serves as the gold standard for diagnosing PRES, since clinical symptoms alone cannot establish a definitive diagnosis. [34] A head computed tomography (CT) scan plays a critical role in evaluating neurologic emergencies that can present with acute-onset altered mentation, headache, and seizures, eg, intracranial hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain without intravenous contrast represents the imaging modality of choice, allowing identification of vasogenic edema, which appears as a hyperintense signal on T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences, thereby improving diagnostic sensitivity. Edema most commonly involves the parieto-occipital lobes but can extend to the temporal lobe, the frontal lobe (superior frontal gyrus), the cerebellum, the brainstem, and the deep white matter. [4] [6] The cortex is often more spared than the white matter due to differences in blood flow regulation, although cortical involvement can occur. [35] [36] MRI also aids in evaluating alternative diagnoses, eg, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, posterior circulation infarct, and primary central nervous system vasculitis. In cases involving the classic posterior cerebral hemispheres, sparing of the calcarine and paramedian occipital regions distinguishes PRES from posterior cerebral artery infarct. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) further differentiates PRES from acute stroke, appearing hypo- or isointense on B1000 sequences. Importantly, restricted diffusion in MRI can occur in a subset of PRES and may reflect cytotoxic edema and ischemic injury rather than purely vasogenic edema. The presence of cytotoxic edema or diffusion restriction has been associated with worse functional outcomes and incomplete reversibility in some cohorts. [37] PRES may also be complicated by intracranial hemorrhage (eg, intraparenchymal hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or microhemorrhages). Hemorrhagic PRES is reported in approximately 17% of cases in pooled analyses and is often associated with poorer outcomes. [38]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Vascular imaging with either CT angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the brain typically appears normal in PRES but can occasionally reveal focal vasoconstriction or vasodilation patterns. [2] Because PRES and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) can overlap clinically and radiographically, angiographic vasoconstriction should also raise the possibility of coexisting RCVS rather than vasculitis alone. [39] Magnetic resonance venography (MRV) also generally appears normal and can help exclude sagittal sinus thrombosis as a potential diagnosis. [40]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Additionally, the evaluation of PRES includes evaluating potential etiologies, which proves crucial for effective management. Laboratory studies can identify imbalances, eg, uremia, hypomagnesemia, hypoalbuminemia, protein deficiency, and hypoglycemia. Lumbar puncture is sometimes performed in immunocompromised patients or when infection is suspected, providing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies that can detect underlying infections, including herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, as well as autoimmune processes.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Electroencephalography (EEG) can assist in patients with PRES, particularly when altered mentation persists without overt tonic, clonic, or tonic-clonic movements, suggesting subclinical seizure activity. EEG patterns, however, generally remain nonspecific for diagnosing PRES. [41]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of PRES requires careful treatment of hypertension along with identification, treatment, and control of the underlying etiology. [5] No specific antihypertensive regimen has been established for acute hypertension associated with PRES. [42] Treatment is recommended when blood pressure exceeds 160/110 mm Hg, with target levels of 130 to 150 mm Hg systolic and 80 to 100 mm Hg diastolic. [33] Rapid or excessive reduction in blood pressure increases the risk of cerebral hypoperfusion and ischemia; therefore, the reduction should not exceed 25% of the presenting blood pressure during the first few hours. [33] Such precise acute management may require admission to an intensive care unit for titratable intravenous antihypertensives, including nicardipine, clevidipine, or labetalol. Transition to oral or nondrip intravenous agents typically follows, with continued blood pressure control on medical floors and in outpatient settings. The duration of postacute antihypertensive therapy remains variable among individuals.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Some patients with PRES develop life-threatening complications, eg, status epilepticus or coma, warranting management in an intensive care unit. [43] No established antiepileptic regimen exists for seizures associated with PRES, and studies defining optimal therapy remain limited; however, levetiracetam and phenytoin commonly serve as treatment options. [42] Antiepileptic therapy may begin during the acute phase and be discontinued after resolution of PRES. [44] In select cases, epilepsy develops and requires long-term antiepileptic treatment. [1]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Clinical practice lacks scientific evidence supporting steroid use for PRES management, despite their theoretical benefit in reducing vasogenic edema. Steroids have also served as triggers for PRES in some individuals receiving treatment for asthma. [45] When PRES associates with immunosuppressive agents, eg, bevacizumab, pazopanib, sorafenib, or sunitinib, dose reduction or substitution of the offending medication remains recommended. [46]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnoses of PRES are broad, including: Intracranial hemorrhage Subdural hemorrhage Subarachnoid hemorrhage Cerebral sinus venous thrombosis Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke Thrombosis of the basilar artery Encephalitis (autoimmune or infectious etiologies like HSV) Uremic encephalopathy Hypoglycemia [2]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: If recognized and treated early, PRES has a favorable prognosis, with symptoms improving within days, weeks, or months. [2] [6] [17] Visual symptoms often resolve completely, especially with early treatment of PRES; however, some cases have reported residual visual deficits (albeit improved) at 3 to 4 months after onset. [31] Although rare, which individuals are at risk of having prolonged visual deficits and persistent seizures is unclear. PRES symptom irreversibility can ensue if treatment is delayed or in cases of significant cerebral edema. [47]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: If the amount of cerebral vasogenic edema is significant, the prognosis can worsen, as the increased pressure on the surrounding blood vessels can compromise blood flow and result in ischemia, stroke, malignant intracranial hypertension, or herniation. [19] [48] In certain situations, prognosis can worsen with involvement of the brainstem and result in death. [19] Recurrence of PRES is possible and has been reported in individuals taking chemotherapy or undergoing dialysis. [2] [49]

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Complications
content: PRES can lead to significant complications, particularly when diagnosis or treatment faces a delay. Although symptoms often improve with timely management, some patients develop permanent neurologic sequelae, including focal deficits, persistent cognitive impairment, or chronic epilepsy. Severe complications include status epilepticus, coma, and ischemic injury resulting from cerebral hypoperfusion or cytotoxic edema. Transforaminal cerebellar herniation represents a life-threatening complication reported in severe cases, especially among pediatric patients following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Complications
content: Visual deficits may persist due to cortical involvement, and recurrent PRES episodes can occur when underlying triggers, eg, uncontrolled hypertension, renal dysfunction, autoimmune disease, or continued exposure to offending medications, remain unaddressed. These complications underscore the importance of early recognition, careful blood pressure management, identification of underlying etiologies, and close neurologic monitoring to reduce morbidity and mortality. [7] [50]
contents: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Complications. Visual deficits may persist due to cortical involvement, and recurrent PRES episodes can occur when underlying triggers, eg, uncontrolled hypertension, renal dysfunction, autoimmune disease, or continued exposure to offending medications, remain unaddressed. These complications underscore the importance of early recognition, careful blood pressure management, identification of underlying etiologies, and close neurologic monitoring to reduce morbidity and mortality. title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence of PRES focuses on early identification and modification of risk factors, particularly strict control of blood pressure and careful monitoring of patients at increased risk. Individuals with chronic hypertension, renal disease, autoimmune conditions, preeclampsia, or exposure to cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapies benefit from regular blood pressure monitoring and timely adjustment of medications to avoid rapid elevations. Clinicians should remain vigilant when initiating or escalating therapies, eg, tacrolimus, chemotherapy agents, or monoclonal antibodies, as early neurologic symptoms may signal the development of PRES. Prompt evaluation of headaches, visual changes, seizures, or altered mental status with appropriate imaging supports early intervention and reduces the likelihood of severe neurologic complications.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education plays a critical role in prevention and early detection. Patients and caregivers should receive clear counseling on recognizing warning signs, eg, new-onset seizures, vision changes, confusion, severe headaches, or sudden blood pressure elevations, and should understand the importance of seeking urgent medical attention if these symptoms occur. Education should also emphasize medication adherence, home blood pressure monitoring when appropriate, and regular follow-up for underlying conditions, eg, hypertension or renal disease. Empowering patients to understand risk factors and early symptoms supports timely care, reduces recurrence, and improves long-term neurologic outcomes. For instance, educating patients about blood pressure management can decrease the likelihood of cerebral autoregulation dysfunction, leading to PRES and other complications. Knowledge of the effects of cytotoxic immunosuppressants on the blood-brain barrier, even in people without hypertension, can help clinicians be more mindful of the risk of PRES in individuals taking these medicines.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: PRES is a clinicoradiographic neurovascular disorder characterized by acute or subacute onset of seizures, encephalopathy, headache, and visual disturbances, most often occurring in the setting of uncontrolled or rapidly rising blood pressure. MRI findings of vasogenic edema, classically involving the parieto-occipital regions but frequently extending beyond posterior circulation territories, support the diagnosis. Although symptoms may resolve with timely treatment, PRES does not guarantee reversibility, and delayed recognition can lead to permanent neurologic deficits, epilepsy, or life-threatening complications. Common risk factors include hypertension, renal disease, autoimmune disorders, sepsis, preeclampsia, and exposure to cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapies, highlighting the need for heightened clinical awareness.

title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal management of PRES relies on coordinated interprofessional care. Physicians, general practitioners, and advanced practitioners require strong diagnostic skills to recognize early clinical patterns, interpret neuroimaging, identify precipitating etiologies, and implement careful blood pressure and seizure management strategies. Nurses play a critical role in continuous neurologic assessment, blood pressure monitoring, seizure observation, and patient education. Pharmacists contribute by optimizing antihypertensive and antiepileptic regimens, monitoring for drug-related triggers, and advising on medication adjustments. Effective interprofessional communication ensures timely escalation of care, safe transitions between inpatient and outpatient settings, and consistent patient education. Collaborative care coordination enhances patient safety, reduces complications, and supports improved neurologic outcomes through shared decision-making and vigilant follow-up.
